content: Genital ulcer disease (GUD) refers to conditions characterized by the presence of ulcerative or pustular lesions in the genital, anal, or perianal regions. These lesions are often caused by sexually transmitted infections (STIs), but they can also result from non-STI-related conditions. Sexually transmitted infections that are commonly associated with GUD include chancroid, genital herpes, donovanosis (also known as granuloma inguinale), lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), and syphilis. In addition to STIs, other non-sexually transmitted conditions can also lead to genital, anal, or perianal lesions. These include genital candidiasis, trauma, carcinoma, aphthae, fixed drug eruptions, psoriasis, and Behçet's disease. It is important to note that sexually transmitted diseases presenting as GUD often share similar clinical manifestations and lesion characteristics. As a result, relying solely on a patient’s medical history and physical examination for diagnosis is frequently inaccurate. Patients presenting with genital, anal, or perianal ulcers should undergo laboratory testing to establish a definitive diagnosis.
